title: Reinforcing versus balancing feedback loops: why retries without backoff take down systems
story:
Two kinds of loop, and almost everything about how a system behaves under stress follows from which one you are in.

The vocabulary comes from system dynamics, created in the mid-1950s by Jay W. Forrester at MIT. He published the first results as a 1958 Harvard Business Review article and expanded them into the field's first book, Industrial Dynamics, in 1961 — developed while studying a General Electric appliance factory, where his simulation showed that management practices rather than market forces were causing its boom-and-bust cycle. That is the shape of the finding to keep: the cycle looked like something happening to the company and was something the company was doing.

Donella Meadows, in Thinking in Systems, gives the two loops their working definitions. Balancing loops are stabilising, goal-seeking and regulating, opposing or reversing whatever direction of change is imposed on the system — sources both of stability and of resistance to change. Reinforcing loops are self-enhancing, leading to exponential growth or runaway collapse, and a system with an unchecked reinforcing loop ultimately will destroy itself.

Now the engineering case, which is the one everybody meets. A database has a brief slowdown. Requests begin timing out. The clients, behaving entirely reasonably, retry. The retries arrive at a database that is already struggling, so more requests time out, so more clients retry. Nothing has failed yet and the load is now climbing on its own, driven by the recovery mechanism. The retry converted a balancing situation — a slow database that would have recovered — into a reinforcing one.

Two of Meadows' observations explain what to do about it. A delay in a balancing loop makes a system likely to oscillate, which is why a fixed retry interval synchronises clients into waves rather than spreading them. And in physical, exponentially growing systems there must be at least one reinforcing loop driving the growth and at least one balancing loop constraining it, because no system can grow forever in a finite environment — so if you have built an amplifier, your job is to supply the constraint deliberately rather than wait for the environment to supply it by breaking.

That is what backoff is. Increasing the delay after each failure converts the amplifier back into something that settles, and randomising it stops the clients arriving together. Neither is a performance optimisation. They are the balancing loop, added on purpose.

problem.name: Loop polarity
problem.shape: A component is under strain and the natural response to strain feeds it.
tell: load climbs while nothing new is arriving from users
a recovery mechanism runs on every failure
clients retry at a fixed interval
the system was fine and then went vertical
problem.move: Establish which kind of loop the response creates before deploying it. Where you have built an amplifier, supply the constraint yourself: increase the delay after each failure so the loop settles, randomise it so clients stop arriving together, and cap the total attempts so the amplification is bounded rather than merely slowed.
problem.invariant: A balancing loop opposes the change imposed on it and settles; a reinforcing loop amplifies it and runs away. The same action can be either, depending on what it feeds.
problem.breaks: The amplifying case is invisible at low load, because a loop that multiplies a small number stays small until it does not. So testing at normal volume cannot distinguish a safe retry policy from a dangerous one — the behaviour only appears at the moment you can least afford to discover it.

cost.time: a failed request now waits longer before being retried, so the recovery a user experiences is slower in exchange for being possible at all
cost.space: per-client retry state, and a cap that must be chosen
cost.beats: immediate retry, which is fastest when nothing is wrong and is the amplifier when something is, and no retry at all, which converts every transient fault into a user-visible failure

worked.problem: Why can retrying a failed request be the thing that takes the system down?
worked.reasoning:
Because the retry is a loop, and under load it is a reinforcing one — the response to strain is more strain, applied by the part of the system that was supposed to be recovering.

Follow the mechanics. A dependency slows briefly. Requests exceed their timeout. Each client, behaving correctly and independently, retries. Those retries arrive at a dependency that is already behind, so service times rise further, so more requests time out, so more retries are issued. The input to the loop is its own output. Nothing has failed, no new users have arrived, and load is climbing on its own.

The framing that makes this legible is the distinction between the two loop types. A balancing loop is stabilising and goal-seeking, opposing or reversing whatever direction of change is imposed — a slow database left alone recovers, because the queue drains faster than it fills once the hiccup passes. A reinforcing loop is self-enhancing, leading to exponential growth or runaway collapse, and a system with an unchecked reinforcing loop ultimately destroys itself. The retry policy is what converts the first situation into the second.

Two further observations tell you what to do. A delay in a balancing loop makes a system likely to oscillate, which is exactly what a fixed retry interval produces: every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment, so the load arrives in synchronised waves rather than spread out. Randomising the delay is the fix, and it is not a micro-optimisation — it is the difference between a smooth queue and a drumbeat.

And in physical, exponentially growing systems there must be at least one reinforcing loop driving growth and at least one balancing loop constraining it, because nothing grows forever in a finite environment. If you have built an amplifier, the constraint is coming whether you choose it or not. Either you supply it — increasing delay, randomised, with a cap on attempts — or the environment supplies it by the system falling over, which is the same constraint arriving in the least useful form.

The part I would emphasise as a warning is that none of this shows up in testing at normal load. A loop that multiplies a small number stays small until it does not. A retry policy that is catastrophic at peak is indistinguishable from a safe one at ordinary volume, which is why this gets discovered during incidents rather than before them.

problem.practice: Find every place your system retries and write down the delay policy for each. Any that retries immediately, or at a fixed interval, is an amplifier waiting for load. Then work out what the total request volume becomes if the dependency stops answering entirely.

beats.broke: A component under strain is helped by the obvious response, and the obvious response feeds the strain — so the thing meant to recover the system is the thing that finishes it.
beats.fix: Identify which kind of loop you are in before acting: one that opposes change and settles, or one that amplifies it. The same action is correct in the first and catastrophic in the second.
beats.cost: The amplifying case is invisible while load is low, since a loop that multiplies a small number stays small until it does not — and by then the growth is the fastest thing in the system.

interview.q: Why can retrying a failed request be the thing that takes the system down?
interview.trap: Treating it as a volume problem to be solved with capacity. The load is being generated by the recovery mechanism itself, so adding capacity extends the ramp rather than stopping it — the fix is to change the loop's polarity, not to feed it.
interview.answer:
